title: The other great languages
hook: your name in your grandmother's mouth and your teacher's: dhamma and dharma are like that
tomorrow: what happens when every piece of the chant is strung together?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last words in Pali: vayadhamma sankhara, appamadena sampadetha. Things fall apart; strive on with care. And there it was again, dhamma, with two m's.
screen: `STRIVE ON WITH CARE.` → `DHAMMA, WITH TWO M'S.`

segments.voice: Your name sounds one way in your grandmother's mouth and another in a substitute teacher's. Nobody thinks there are two of you. Buddhist words travel like that. A book says dharma; a chant says dhamma. A poster says nirvana; a sutta says nibbana. So which spelling is right? Both. They're the same word in two old languages, Sanskrit and Pali, and once you hear the pattern, you can hear it in your own mouth.
screen: `ONE NAME, TWO MOUTHS.` → `DHARMA OR DHAMMA?` → `BOTH. SAME WORD.`

segments.voice: Put them side by side. Sanskrit dharma, Pali dhamma. Nirvana, nibbana. Karma, kamma. Sutra, sutta. Maitri, metta. Hear it? Where Sanskrit stacks two different sounds together, Pali often smooths them into one doubled sound: the r drops out, the m doubles. Two spellings, one word. Then the words kept traveling, and in some languages they weren't respelled at all; they were translated. In Tibetan, the dharma is chö and the Buddha is sangye. In Chinese, the dharma is fa and the Buddha is fo. Vietnamese says Phap and Phat. And sometimes a sound rides along almost whole. The namo at the start of the homage, homage to him, turns up in a Vietnamese temple as nam mo, before the name of a Buddha. Same bow, a different mouth. None of this makes one spelling the real one. Theravada chanting keeps the Pali; Sanskrit forms fill Mahayana books. Tibetan and Chinese and Vietnamese speakers say it in their own. It's a little like what the Buddha told his monks at the start of this block: learn it in your own dialect.
screen: `DHARMA, DHAMMA. NIRVANA, NIBBANA.` · `PALI SMOOTHS, DOUBLES.` · `TIBETAN CHÖ, CHINESE FA.` · `NAMO BECOMES NAM MO.` · then, large: `TWO SPELLINGS, ONE WORD.`

segments.voice: Say each pair out loud, slowly: dharma, dhamma; nirvana, nibbana; karma, kamma. Feel where each one lives: the r rolling behind the teeth, the doubled m pressing the lips. Then let the sounds go and sit with the one meaning under both.
The other great languages: Sanskrit beside Pali, and Tibetan, Chinese and Vietnamese after them. One teaching, many mouths.
Hold on to this: two spellings, one word, and more mouths than that. Twenty-seven of twenty-nine.

screen: `DAY 1453 COUNTS.` → `A LITTLE PALI · 27 OF 29.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT HAPPENS WHEN EVERY PIECE IS STRUNG TOGETHER?`

howItsDone: Theravada temples chant in Pali; Tibetan, Chinese, Japanese, Korean and Vietnamese Buddhists chant in their own languages or in old sound-forms of Sanskrit names, and English books mix Pali and Sanskrit spellings.

notes: Pali/Sanskrit pairs follow the PTS dictionary. 'Pali often smooths [clusters] into one doubled sound' is a general description of assimilation (rm>mm, rv>bb); stated with 'often'; confirm.

Tibetan chö (chos) for dharma and sangye (sangs rgyas) for Buddha; Chinese fa (法) for dharma and fo (佛) for Buddha; Vietnamese Pháp and Phật: written in the voice without diacritics or characters (Phap, Phat) for the narrator; confirm spellings. No derivation claim is made for fo or Phật.

'Namo … turns up in a Vietnamese temple as nam mo (Nam mô), before the name of a Buddha' (e.g. Nam mô A Di Đà Phật): the link between Pali/Sanskrit namo and Vietnamese nam mô is a sound-borrowing via Chinese; stated plainly as 'a sound rides along'. Confirm with a Vietnamese Buddhist reader.
'Sanskrit forms fill Mahayana books' describes usage without a count.
Gloss scripts: only Devanagari is allowed for this path, so Tibetan, Chinese and Vietnamese glosses carry meaning and sound only. Gloss key 'nam mo' matches the voice spelling.
The closing callback to 'learn it in your own dialect' (day 1427, Cullavagga V.33.1) is framed 'a little like', not as the Buddha speaking about Tibetan or Chinese.
